clue.text: A doctor is about to see feet

definitions.note: plural metrical units, matching a plural answer

indicators.note: about means the word is wraps around the other pieces, as if circling them

parts.note: MB is Bachelor of Medicine, a doctor's degree

explanation.surface: Someone is told a doctor is coming round to look at their feet.
explanation.walkthrough: The feet are units of verse, not body parts; MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is the doctor, and 'to see' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An iamb is a metrical foot of one short and one long syllable, so several are poetic feet.

clue.text: Officer at first governing normally

indicators.note: at first means the governing word is placed before the officer

parts.note: a party in power is said to be in
a general is a senior army officer

explanation.surface: An officer who initially ruled in the usual way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at first' puts IN, for governing, as in a party being in power, ahead of GENERAL.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means as a rule or usually.

clue.text: So-called style of house

indicators.note: so-called here means the word is called out, said rather than spelt

parts.note: a style or way of doing things is a manner

explanation.surface: The name of an architectural style of house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'So-called' marks the sound: MANNER said aloud gives the grand house.
explanation.definitionFit: A manor is a country estate's main residence.

clue.text: Snuff is mellower, nonetheless

definitions.note: a verb, to put out a flame

indicators.note: read as none-the-less, it means the O for none is taken away

parts.note: smoother means softer and more mellow

explanation.surface: Snuff is gentler on the nose, all the same.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'nonetheless' as 'none less': O, a zero or none, comes out of SMOOTHER. Snuff is the verb to extinguish, not tobacco.
explanation.definitionFit: To snuff a candle is to extinguish it by cutting off its air.

clue.text: Copper wire's not untidy when sheathed

indicators.note: a sheathed thing is enclosed, so the wire word wraps round the jumbled letters

parts.note: a cable is a thick wire

indicators.note: untidy letters are in disorder, so the S of the apostrophe and not are mixed up

explanation.surface: An electrician remarks that a copper wire looks neat once it is insulated.
explanation.walkthrough: The S comes from the apostrophe-s of wire's, jumbled by 'untidy' with not; 'when sheathed' is the container signal. Copper is the policeman, not the metal.
explanation.definitionFit: Copper is British slang for a police officer, and a constable is the lowest rank of officer.

clue.text: One receiving social benefit in small measure is right to hold on

indicators.note: in means one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: CT is the abbreviation for carat, a small unit of weight
a lien is a legal right to keep property until a debt is paid

explanation.surface: A benefit claimant, in a modest way, is entitled to keep what they have.
explanation.walkthrough: A lien is a legal right to retain goods until a debt is settled; carat is the small measure, 'in' the container signal and 'is' a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A social worker calls the person they help a client, someone who receives a service.

clue.text: Old raider calls boy up

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the whole run is read from bottom to top

parts.note: to call someone something is to name them
Ron is a boy's name

explanation.surface: A Viking summons a lad upstairs.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'up' reads the pieces from the bottom, so the whole charade comes out backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Viking raiders from Scandinavia were known as men of the north.

clue.text: Argument over some muslin

indicators.note: in a down entry, over puts the argument word above the next piece

parts.note: a tiff is a petty quarrel
any and some are interchangeable in many sentences

explanation.surface: A squabble over a piece of fine cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'over' means the first piece sits on top of the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiffany is a thin, gauzy silk or muslin fabric.

clue.text: Legendary murderer with dirty hair

parts.note: blue means risqué or smutty, as in a blue joke
a beard is facial hair

explanation.surface: A notorious killer of folk tale had grubby hair.
explanation.walkthrough: Dirty means smutty, not grimy; 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: In Perrault's folk tale he murders each of his wives in turn.

clue.text: Guard failing to open gate

indicators.note: a word failing to open lacks its opening letter

parts.note: a sentry is a soldier on guard

explanation.surface: A guard cannot get the gate to open.
explanation.walkthrough: 'failing to open' removes the first letter of SENTRY.
explanation.definitionFit: A gate is a way in, a synonym for an entrance.

clue.text: Giuseppe, for example, drooling idiotically about the end of Venice

definitions.note: Giuseppe Palmieri is a character in Gilbert and Sullivan's The Gondoliers

indicators.note: about here means the jumbled letters go round the single letter
done idiotically, the letters of drooling are scrambled
the end of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: An Italian man is seen slobbering foolishly somewhere around Venice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'idiotically' rearranges DROOLING, and 'about' wraps those letters round E, 'the end of Venice'. Giuseppe is one of the two boatmen heroes of The Gondoliers, a Gilbert and Sullivan comic opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Giuseppe is one of the boatman heroes of Gilbert and Sullivan's opera set in Venice, an example of that trade.

clue.text: During Lent, university produces German drama

indicators.note: something happening during a period sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: Lent is a time of fasting, so it gives fast

explanation.surface: A university stages a German play in the Lenten season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'During' puts U inside FAST; Lent is the Christian season of fasting.
explanation.definitionFit: Goethe's verse play about a scholar who sells his soul is the most famous German drama.

clue.text: Miss Morland longed for this: grant her one baby to rock

definitions.note: Catherine Morland, the heroine of Jane Austen's novel, dreams of visiting the old abbey of the title

indicators.note: rocking shakes things about, so these letters are reordered

explanation.surface: A woman named Morland yearns for a child and is told she will be granted one to cradle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to rock' rearranges GRANT HER ONE BABY. In Jane Austen's novel the heroine, Catherine Morland, longs to see the Gothic abbey that gives the book its title.
explanation.definitionFit: In Austen's novel the heroine, steeped in Gothic romances, yearns to be invited to the ancient Tilney family abbey.

clue.text: Profit from ticket

explanation.surface: Someone makes money out of a ticket.
explanation.definitionFit: A return is the yield on an investment, and also a ticket for an outward and back journey.

clue.text: Way of handling meat that's rotten — put it in the river

indicators.note: put it in means the jumbled meat goes inside the river

parts.note: the Trent is a major river in the English Midlands

indicators.note: rotten meat has broken down, so its letters are disordered

explanation.surface: Advice on dealing with spoilt meat: dump it in the river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that's rotten' scrambles the meat and 'put it in' places it inside the Trent, a river in the English Midlands, which is split by it.
explanation.definitionFit: How something is handled or dealt with is its treatment.

clue.text: Queen to arrive in state

parts.note: Mary was the name of several English and Scottish queens
to land is to arrive, as a plane does

explanation.surface: A queen arrives in grand style for an official visit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is only a link; state means a US state, not pomp.
explanation.definitionFit: Maryland is one of the United States, on the Atlantic coast.

clue.text: Newspaper excluding esoteric subject

indicators.note: excluding means those letters are left out of the newspaper

parts.note: The Independent is a British national newspaper
in means known only to insiders, as in an in-joke

explanation.surface: A paper leaves out an obscure topic.
explanation.walkthrough: The Independent is a British national daily. 'excluding' drops IN, 'in' in the sense of an in-joke known only to a few. Subject is an adjective, as in subject to.
explanation.definitionFit: Being subject to a ruler means being reliant on or under the control of another.

clue.text: Brief in a hard case like this

definitions.text: Brief in a hard case like this

parts.words: Brief in a hard case like this
parts.note: a phrase meaning briefly uses the shell of a nut, a hard case

explanation.surface: A lawyer's brief stored in a tough case.
explanation.walkthrough: Brief looks like a legal document, but 'in a ___' is the idiom for put briefly, and the word is literally a hard casing.
explanation.definitionFit: To put it briefly is to say it in a few words; the shell of a nut is a hard case.

clue.text: Relax with story before a contest

parts.note: a story can be a fib or lie
a bout is a contest, as in boxing

explanation.surface: Someone unwinds with a tale before a match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' and 'before' only arrange the pieces in order.
explanation.definitionFit: To idle or lounge around doing nothing is to take it easy.

clue.text: Hearing the sound of surf from Sydney beach, I dropped out with husband

definitions.note: said aloud, surf sounds like serf, a peasant bound to the land

indicators.note: dropped out means that letter leaves the beach name

parts.note: Bondi is a famous beach in Sydney
man as in man and wife

explanation.surface: A man hears the waves at Bondi, gives up and goes home with his husband.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition works by sound: surf heard is serf. BONDI loses I ('I dropped out'), then MAN; 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A serf or slave bound to service is a bondman.

clue.text: It's tough at university to be short of money

parts.note: tough and hard are synonyms
up means in residence at a university, as in up at Oxford

explanation.surface: A student finds it hard being broke at college.
explanation.walkthrough: Being 'up' is the British idiom for being at a university, especially Oxford or Cambridge.
explanation.definitionFit: Being strapped for cash is the plain meaning of the idiom.

clue.text: Cause surprise in the matter of a German connection

parts.note: as to means concerning
und is German for and, a connecting word

explanation.surface: Something startling about a German link.
explanation.walkthrough: 'connection' means a conjunction: German und, 'and'.
explanation.definitionFit: To amaze is to strike someone with surprise.

clue.text: Sank like shrimps, maybe

explanation.surface: Something went down like shellfish.
explanation.definitionFit: To sink a ball in snooker is to pot it; preserved in a jar with butter is how shrimps are often sold.

clue.text: Refuse to speed?

explanation.surface: A question of whether someone declines to drive fast.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to take a firm stand and say no, and literally to press hard on the accelerator.

clue.text: Take one step off the track

indicators.note: off means the letters are knocked out of order

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Advice to step off the path.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take' is a link; 'off' rearranges I and STEP.
explanation.definitionFit: A ski run or fencing strip is called a piste.

clue.text: Map-makers' alias for Japanese city

parts.note: OS is the Ordnance Survey, Britain's official map-makers
aka stands for also known as, introducing an alias

explanation.surface: A cartographers' other name for a city in Japan.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ordnance Survey (OS) is Britain's national mapping agency.
explanation.definitionFit: Osaka is a major port city in Japan.

clue.text: Cook's energy

explanation.surface: A chef's vigour in the kitchen.
explanation.definitionFit: To cook food over boiling water is one sense; vapour power, as in running out of puff, is the other.

clue.text: Associates have fallen out in anger

definitions.note: a plural noun for a group of companions, matching a collective answer

indicators.note: in means one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: to anger someone is to enrage them

indicators.note: fallen here means tumbled about, so the letters of out are muddled

explanation.surface: Colleagues have had a row and are furious.
explanation.walkthrough: Anger is a verb here, not a noun; 'fallen' scrambles out and 'in' places it inside, while 'have' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A retinue is the group of people who accompany someone important.

clue.text: Gentle and moving, but not straightforward

indicators.note: moving letters are shifted around into a new order

explanation.surface: A piece is described as tender and touching, though complicated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moving' looks like a description, but it rearranges GENTLE AND.
explanation.definitionFit: Something knotted or complicated is not simple or direct.

clue.text: Distributed among wide alternatives

indicators.note: among says the letters sit within the words that follow

explanation.surface: Something was shared out across a broad range of options.
explanation.definitionFit: Cards are handed out to players, so to give out shares is a synonym.
